evidence: src/domain/entities/Project.ts: `static create(id, name, description)` trims the name and throws ValidationError('Project name must not be empty'); the constructor is private.
src/domain/entities/User.ts: `static create(id, name)` trims the name and throws ValidationError('User name must not be empty'); the constructor is private.
src/domain/entities/Task.ts: `static create(props: NewTaskProps)` trims the title and throws ValidationError; `markDone()` uses TaskStatus.isDone() and TaskStatus.DONE and throws ConflictError.

src/domain/entities/Task.ts: `assignTo(userId)` says in its doc comment that callers must ensure the user exists (see TaskAssignmentService), so the check that needs a repository stays in one domain service.
All three entities import their errors from ../errors/DomainErrors, so they share one error abstraction.
parsedVerdict.reasoning:
The three files form one coherent unit: Project, User and Task are all domain entities. Each has a private constructor and a static `create` factory that checks its own invariants and throws the shared domain errors (ValidationError, ConflictError). Task uses the value objects TaskStatus and DueDate in a consistent way.

The "trim, then reject empty" check appears in Project.create, User.create and Task.create. However, each check enforces a different entity's own invariant (project name, user name, task title) with its own message. That is a repeated pattern, not one rule that should live in a single place, though a shared NonEmptyName value object could be considered.

Task.assignTo hands the "assigned user must exist" check to TaskAssignmentService, as its doc comment says. That check needs a repository lookup, so keeping it in a domain service is an accepted design rather than a bypass of the module's abstractions. It still lives in one place. Nothing in the unit splits into unrelated concerns or skips the module's factories or value objects.
